title: Stability-oriented load emulator and randomized priming procedures
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a design and practical procedures for a stability-first load emulator and randomized priming protocol. The goal is to reduce brittle benchmark outcomes caused by deterministic client sequencing, prefix-cache artifacts, and thermal/occupancy hysteresis. We want repeatable throughput baselines while preserving a realistic degree of stochasticity so experiments better reflect production variance.

Scope and goals
- Provide an emulator design that produces realistic arrival patterns and realistic sequence-length mixes for our inference stack.
- Define a multi-phase priming/warmup procedure that avoids over-priming and yields stable post-warmup metrics.
- Give concrete loadgen config examples and statistical checks to assert run repeatability.
- Capture troubleshooting guidance for when runs diverge unexpectedly.

Assumptions and context
- Target: throughput experiments for models served by the runtime (quantized and fp16 paths).
- Hardware heterogeneity is present (A100/T4-like cluster mix); warmup interacts with microstate allocation and kernel selection.
- Prefix caching / KV cache makes early responses faster; naive priming produces optimistic throughput.
- We expect ~10-40% day-to-day variance in production arrival patterns; harness should surface stable capacity numbers while not hiding variance.

High-level approach
1) Emulate per-client session semantics rather than stateless firehose where appropriate. Sessions mean KV cache reuse and token distribution similar to production.
2) Randomize sequence order and inter-arrival times across seed-controlled runs to prevent order bias.
3) Multi-phase priming: short chaotic primer -> controlled ramp -> stabilization window -> measurement window.
4) Use statistical tests (KS, CIs, bootstrapping) across replicate runs to judge repeatability.

Emulator design details
- Client semantics: represent N concurrent clients, each submitting a sequence stream with per-session randomness (sequence length, user prefix distribution). Implement client affinity so subsequent requests from same client reuse cache with configurable probability p_reuse.
- Sequence catalog: maintain a catalog of templates (short prompts, long-context, chat style). Draw sequences using a weighted distribution matching observed production fingerprint (use offline telemetry to populate weights).
- Inter-arrival modeling: support pluggable arrival kernels: exponential (Poisson), Weibull (for burstiness), and an empirical arrival distribution captured from production. Allow configurable jitter: per-request jitter sampled from uniform +/- X% to avoid synchronized bursts.
- Tokenization and response size: sample response length from an empirical PMF. This ensures batching and GPU occupancy effects replicate real runs.

Randomization and seed hygiene
- Each run is created with an explicit RNG seed logged at start. Seeds control: sequence order, arrival times, client assignment, and token length sampling.
- To analyze sensitivity, run small experiment sets that vary only the seed (e.g., 10 seeds). If between-seed variance dominates, the workload is inherently noisy; increase replicate count or tighten arrival model.
- Never hardcode a single deterministic order for production-like benchmarking; preserves false precision.

Priming/warmup protocol (recommended)
Phase A — Primer (60–180s):
- Purpose: activate compilation/kernels, L2 warming, initial device memory allocation.
- Use high-entropy randomized short sequences at 1.5x expected concurrency to exercise code paths.
Phase B — Stabilized ramp (3–8 minutes):
- Linearly ramp to target concurrency over 3–8 minutes using the real arrival distribution. This prevents thermal shocks and sudden kernel-switching artifacts.
- Monitor GPU microstate (util, mem) and runtime logs for first allocation or JIT events.
Phase C — Pre-measure stabilization (2–5 minutes):
- Hold at target concurrency but only collect lightweight telemetry (no heavy aggregation). Check metrics converge: variance of 1s throughput samples drops below configured threshold (e.g., 5%).
Phase D — Measurement window (5–15 minutes):
- Collect detailed metrics: per-request latency distribution, tail latencies (p50/p95/p99), compute time breakdown, power/thermal if available, kernel selection histogram, CPU-side scheduling times, and batch sizes.
- Record trace logs for a configurable fraction of requests (e.g., 1%) to capture KV cache state and path decisions.

Why multi-phase?
- Single-shot warmups either under- or over-prime. Primer exercises code heterogeneity; ramp avoids hysteresis-induced oscillations; stabilization verifies metric convergence before measurement.

Measurement and repeatability checks
- Replicates: at least 5 independent runs with distinct seeds for baseline. For noisy workloads increase to 10+.
- Metrics to compare across replicates: median throughput, p95 latency, average batch size, kernel selection distribution.
- Statistical tests:
  - Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test on latency CDFs to detect distributional shifts between runs.
  - Confidence intervals via bootstrapping on throughput samples (1s or 5s buckets). Require overlap of CI across majority of replicates for stability.
  - ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis on throughput samples to test whether between-seed variance is larger than within-seed noise.
- Repeatability gate: define an experiment pass if across at least 70% of replicates: throughput CI overlap and KS p-value > 0.05 between pairs (or adjusted for multiple comparisons). Adjust thresholds per SLO needs.

Example loadgen configuration (YAML-like pseudoconfig)
- name: stability-emulator-run
  clients: 128
  concurrency_target: 1024
  arrival_kernel: weibull # options: poisson, empirical, weibull
  arrival_params: {k: 1.3, lambda: 0.02}
  sequence_catalog: production_fingerprint_v3
  reuse_probability: 0.42
  primer: {duration_s: 120, concurrency_multiplier: 1.5}
  ramp: {duration_s: 300, method: linear}
  stabilization: {duration_s: 180, variance_threshold_pct: 5}
  measurement: {duration_s: 600, trace_sample_rate: 0.01}
  rng_seed: 1849271 # override per replicate

Notes on config knobs
- reuse_probability controls how often a client reuses the same session/KV cache. Lower values simulate more cold starts.
- concurrency_target indicates aggregate parallel in-flight requests; clients divide work based on per-client pacing.
- trace_sample_rate should be low to avoid perturbing performance but high enough to capture path diversity.

Observability and required signals
- Per-request: request id, client id, seed, sequence id, request size (tokens), response size, latency (split: client->runtime, runtime queuing, runtime compute, post-processing).
- Runtime internals: kernel variant chosen, batch size, GPU util, GPU memory usage, memory alloc events, and KV cache hit/miss counters.
- System: CPU steal, network IO, host thermal headroom.
- External: when running dedicated clusters, collect node-level telemetry to correlate with scheduler events.

Failure modes and troubleshooting checklist
- Non-converging stabilization window:
  - Check for JIT or compilation events happening after ramp; increase primer length or add dedicated compiler primer step.
  - Inspect batch size heatmap; large swings indicate client pacing misconfiguration.
- High between-seed variance:
  - Increase number of replicates.
  - Compare sequence catalog composition across seeds; if a rare long sequence creates high variance, consider weighted sampling adjustments.
- System noise spikes:
  - Correlate with node-level telemetry for background jobs, eviction events, or cloud host maintenance.

Experiment catalogue (minimum to run for a new model onboarding)
1) Primer length sweep: primer {30,60,120,300}s while keeping ramp/stabilization constant. Observe where compiler and kernel events stop appearing in measurement window.
2) Seed sensitivity: 10 seeds at nominal config; compute CI overlap and KS tests.
3) Reuse probability sweep: {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} to understand cache sensitivity to session locality.
4) Arrival kernel impact: poisson vs weibull vs empirical; measure p95 and throughput delta.
5) Concurrency ramp rate: fast vs slow ramps to detect hysteresis threshold.

Expected artifacts per experiment
- Raw request logs (compressed), one file per replicate
- Aggregated 1s/5s throughput buckets as CSV
- Latency CDFs and KS/ANOVA output summary (text)
- Small trace sample recording in JSONL (1% of requests)
- Run metadata: config file, RNG seed, git sha of bench harness, runtime version, model version, hardware inventory file

Appendix A — quick checklist before a run
- Toggle off autoscaling or ensure cluster capacity pinned for experiment duration.
- Drain tenant traffic or isolate test cluster.
- Ensure bench harness binary/githash and runtime container images recorded.
- Pre-pull images, pre-warm disk caches.
- Confirm time sync across hosts (NTP), and confirm clock skew < 2ms to avoid bucket misalignment.

Appendix B — short sample analysis recipe
1) For each replicate, compute mean throughput and 95% bootstrap CI using 1s buckets.
2) Plot overlayed latency CDFs and run KS test between each pair.
3) If CIs do not overlap, flag run and inspect traces for outliers (long tail sequences, misshapen batch sizes).
4) Create a run narrative: what compiler events occurred, did any host report errors, kernel fallback events.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Evaluate whether primer should preferentially exercise the slowest code paths (e.g., long-context attention) or be uniformly random — initial hypothesis: primer should overweight rare heavy paths to avoid late-run surprises.
- Add automated detection for late JIT/compilation events that would fail a run early.
- Integrate thermal-aware ramp (slower ramps when GPU temperature delta exceeds threshold).
